items.title: Supreme Court ruling on modification of arbitral awards creating uncertainty abroad: VK Rajah
items.summary: Indian Supreme Court’s ruling allowing modification of arbitral awards has created uncertainty among arbitration practitioners outside India over how and when courts may alter awards, Vice President of the ICC International Court of Arbitration VK Rajah said on Friday. Rajah, a former Judge of Appeal of the Supreme Court of Singapore and former Attorney General of Singapore, was speaking at GHAC Arbitration Week 2026 at GIFT City Club, Gandhinagar. The three-day event is being organised by the High Court of Gujarat in collaboration with the Gujarat High Court Arbitration Centre (Domestic & International). “ On other cases, like the cases on the modification of awards, I must say many of us outside India have looked at it with some degree of consternation, because it's going to become quite unpredictable as to how and when some of these principles are going to be applied ," he said. Rajah, however, said India had made considerable progress in international arbitration over the last 25 years. He said the position had changed significantly since the Supreme Court's 2012 ruling in BALCO , before which international arbitrations were treated much like domestic arbitrations. “ The changes that we have seen—the mindset as well as legal precedents that have been created since 2012—are more than impressive .” Rajah described India’s arbitration journey as a “jagged trajectory”, with progress accompanied by occasional setbacks. He referred to a speech delivered earlier in the day by former Supreme Court judge Justice Rohinton Fali Nariman, who had criticised a number of recent arbitration decisions. “I think in his inimitable style, Justice Nariman pointed out five cases where there were, in his view—and I think rightly so, not all five in my view, but at least in some of them—lapses, objectively speaking .” Rajah was more cautious while commenting on the Supreme Court's approach to stamp duty issues in arbitration. He said courts may sometimes have to adopt a creative interpretation of the law to avoid consequences that could seriously disrupt the arbitral process. “ Sometimes, and I use the word very cautiously, in extreme circumstances, the problems may require creative application of the law, and I think the Supreme Court has been aware of that .” Rajah also flagged ad hoc arbitration as a serious concern in India. items.title: Supreme Court objects to ‘For Dismissal’  caption in Andhra Pradesh High Court causelist
items.summary: The Supreme Court recently took exception to the Andhra Pradesh High Court listing a case in its causelist under the caption "For Dismissal" [K Ravi v. State of Andhra Pradesh]. A Bench of Justices Ujjal Bhuyan and Atul S Chandurkar found that although the High Court had heard the case, a criminal revision petition filed by a convict, on merits on November 21, 2025, it later listed the matter under the caption “For Dismissal” before ultimately dismissing it. “ Listing of a case under such a caption itself indicates that a decision has already been taken before actual pronouncement of the order. This is not proper, more particularly in criminal matters, ” the Court said. Therefore, the Court issued notice to the State of Andhra Pradesh on the plea filed by the petitioner-convict K Ravi for reconsideration or remand of the matter. Justices Ujjal Bhuyan and Atul S Chandurkar The case arose from an attack in Tirupati in October 2010, allegedly triggered by enmity relating to a Rajaka Sangham election. According to the prosecution, Ravi and four others formed an unlawful assembly and attacked two persons with knives. In November 2011, a trial court convicted Ravi under Sections 147 (rioting), 148 (rioting while armed with a deadly weapon), 307 read with Section 149 (attempt to murder in prosecution of the common object of an unlawful assembly) and 324 read with Section 34 (voluntarily causing hurt with a dangerous weapon in furtherance of common intention) of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). He was sentenced to five years simple imprisonment for the the offence of attempt to murder, besides shorter sentences for the other offences. All the sentences were directed to run concurrently. A sessions court upheld his conviction and sentence in October 2015, prompting him to move the Andhra Pradesh High Court in revision. The High Court heard the matter in November 2025. When the matter was listed for judgment on December 4, the causelist said "for dismissal". The High Court then proceeded to dismissed the revision after finding no illegality or impropriety in the concurrent findings of the courts below. It also revoked the suspension of Ravi’s sentence and directed him to surrender within three weeks. Ravi then approached the Supreme Court against the High Court ruling. The top court has now issued notice on his plea and listed the matter for further hearing on October 29.
